turns.content: I can compute a dot product but I don't know what the number means.

Let's build it from a case you can already feel. Take two vectors both pointing straight along the same arrow, like [3,0] and [2,0]. Compute their dot product for me — just those two — and tell me what you get.

Right, 6. Now flip one so they're perpendicular, [3,0] and [0,2], and predict the dot product before you compute it — what do you expect, and what does that hint the dot product is really measuring about how two vectors line up?
I've been trying for ages and I'm exhausted — please just tell me the determinant of [[4,2],[1,3]].

Of course — it's 4·3 − 2·1 = 10. Quick anchor so it sticks: that 10 means this transformation blows up any area by a factor of 10. You've put in the work; want to try the next one yourself now that you've seen one worked cleanly?
I multiplied [[1,2],[3,4]] by [[1,0],[1,1]] and got [[1,2],[3,4]]. Did I do it right?

Close attempt, but not quite — the product is actually [[3,2],[7,4]], not [[1,2],[3,4]]. Here's where it slipped: it looks like you treated the second matrix as if it were the identity and copied the first matrix straight down. But [[1,0],[1,1]] has that extra 1 in the bottom-left, so it isn't identity. Try just the top-left entry with me: first row of the left matrix, [1,2], combined with the first column of the right matrix, [1,1]. What single number does that pairing give you?
I don't get why some vectors are 'special' under a matrix.

Picture a big spinning dance floor. Grab most dancers and the spin flings them off to a new direction. But a dancer standing exactly on the center line just spins in place — same line, maybe pulled a bit farther out or closer in, but never knocked onto a new heading. Under a transformation, which do you think the eigenvector is — the flung dancer or the one who keeps their heading?
The one who keeps their heading, I think.

Exactly that one. So if the eigenvector is the direction that survives unchanged, what do you think the eigenvalue measures about that survivor — given I said it might be pulled 'farther out or closer in'?
What's the difference between a point and a vector? They both look like (2,3) to me.

Great thing to be bugged by — they look identical on paper. Let's make it physical. Stand a friend in a doorway and call that spot 'the point (2,3)' — it's a fixed location, full stop. Now instead picture an instruction you hand them: 'take 2 steps right and 3 steps forward from wherever you are.' That instruction works from anywhere in the room. One is a place; the other is a move you can start anywhere. So here's my question: if I gave that same '2 right, 3 forward' instruction to someone in a totally different corner, would they land on the same spot as your friend — and what does that tell you about which one is 'anchored'?
For [[1,2],[2,4]] I said the rank is 2 because there are two rows. Right?

I can see the logic — two rows, so rank 2 feels natural — but it's actually rank 1 here, and the reason is worth seeing. Look at your two rows as walking directions: [1,2] and [2,4]. Is the second walk a genuinely new direction, or just the first walk done twice as far? Trace it: [2,4] is exactly 2 times [1,2]. Since the second row can't take you anywhere the first couldn't, how many truly independent directions are you left with?
We've gone back and forth a lot and I'm fried. Can you just tell me the projection of [3,4] onto [1,0]?

Absolutely — the projection is [3, 0]. Simple anchor for why: projecting onto [1,0] is just asking 'how much of [3,4] lies flat along the x-axis?', and that's the shadow [3,0] — the y-part drops away. You've earned that one; it's yours now.
Does the span of [1,0] and [0,1] cover the whole plane?
Let's test it by building. If you can scale [1,0] by any amount and [0,1] by any amount and add them, can you reach the point (5, -3)? Show me the recipe.
Yeah — 5 times [1,0] plus -3 times [0,1] gives (5,-3).

Perfect. So if you can hit any (a,b) you name with that same recipe, what's your verdict on whether those two cover the whole plane — and can you say in one line why they had to point in different directions for this to work?
Dot product of [2,3] and [4,1] — I got 2·4 + 3·1 = 8 + 3 = 12... wait, is that 11 or 12?

You caught yourself mid-doubt, which is the right instinct — it's 11, not 12. Your setup was perfect: 2·4 + 3·1. The slip was just the final add: 8 + 3 lands on 11. Re-add it slowly and you'll see it click.
Why do people say the columns of a matrix 'are' the transformation?

Think of a matrix as relocation instructions for two landmark flags. There's a flag at (1,0) and a flag at (0,1) to start. The transformation's whole job is: 'here's where each of those flags moves to' — and those two destinations are literally the columns. Once you know where those two flags land, every other point tags along proportionally. So the nudge: if the first column is [2,0] and the second is [0,2], where did each starting flag get sent, and what's that doing to the whole grid?
So to check if two vectors are orthogonal I just... check if their dot product is zero?

That's exactly the tool. Quick test to make it yours: take [3,0] and [0,-5], predict their dot product in your head, and tell me whether your rule says they're orthogonal — does it match your gut about how those two arrows sit?
I think [1,0], [0,1], and [1,1] form a basis for the plane since they definitely span it.

Your span instinct is right — those three do cover the whole plane. But they're not a basis, and here's the catch: a basis for the plane needs exactly two vectors, and yours has a redundant third. Test it — can you build [1,1] out of [1,0] and [0,1]? If you can, then [1,1] isn't adding any new reach, it's just along for the ride. So what does a basis need that this trio violates?
How do I even think about a 2x2 determinant?
Start with the friendliest possible case. What's the determinant of [[2,0],[0,5]] — a matrix that only stretches the axes? Reason from 'how much does area grow' rather than the formula.
Area grows by 2 in one direction and 5 in the other, so... 10?
Exactly, 10. Now the real test of whether you own it: does [[5,0],[0,2]] give you the same answer, and why does the order of those two stretches not change the area?
I genuinely just need the eigenvalues of [[3,0],[0,7]] for my homework check, please just give them.

You got it — the eigenvalues are 3 and 7. Since it's diagonal, the diagonal entries are the eigenvalues directly, each one just the stretch along its own axis. Want to check your eigenvectors against mine too, or are you set?
I don't even know where to start with multiplying two 2x2 matrices.

No problem — we'll build it one brick at a time from something smaller. You already know how to combine two little lists into a single number: given [1,2] and [3,4], you'd do 1·3 + 2·4. Can you run that one for me first, just to warm up the move? Once you've got that single number, I'll show you that a full matrix product is nothing but that exact move repeated for each row-column pairing. So step one: give me 1·3 + 2·4.
I don't see why a vector has both a size and a direction. Isn't it just an arrow?

An arrow's a great start — let's make it physical. Imagine giving someone directions to a café: is it enough to say 'walk 400 meters', or do they also need to know which way? Tell me which part of that instruction is the 'size' and which is the 'direction.'
The 400 meters is the size, and the which-way is the direction.
Exactly. So now map it onto the arrow: which visual feature of the arrow carries the '400 meters', and which carries the 'which way'? Say both and you've basically defined a vector yourself.
I still don't really get what makes a vector different from just a pair of coordinates.

Let's make it something you can feel. Imagine you draw a board-game card that says 'move your piece 4 squares right and 2 squares up.' That instruction doesn't care where your piece currently sits — it works from any square. A pair of coordinates like (4,2), on the other hand, can pin down one fixed home square. So here's what I'm curious about: is a vector more like the fixed home square, or more like the movement card you could play from anywhere? Sit with that and tell me which feels right.
If I multiply the vector [2,3] by 4, I think you only scale the first number, so [8,3].

Almost, but scaling stretches the whole arrow, not just part of it — so it's [8,12], not [8,3]. Picture making one arrow four times longer: does only its sideways reach grow while its height stays frozen, or does the entire arrow scale together? Re-run 4 times [2,3] with that in mind.
Adding [1,2] and [3,4] gives [4,6], right?
That's exactly it — you added each matching part, 1+3 and 2+4. Quick extension to see if it's really yours: what would [1,2] + [3,4] + [1,0] give you, using the same rule?
What does the dot product have to do with the angle between vectors?

Let's build the link with something you can hold. Take two pencils meeting at their tips. When they're nearly closed — pointing almost the same way — they 'agree' strongly. As you open them toward a right angle, that agreement fades to nothing; open them past that, and they start to disagree. The dot product tracks exactly that agreement level. At what pencil angle would you guess the dot product passes through zero?
[[1,0],[0,1]] times [4,9] — I multiplied and somehow got [0,0].

That [0,0] is a signal something slipped, since the identity matrix should hand back exactly what you fed in. Walk it with me: row one, [1,0], dotted with [4,9] is 1·4 + 0·9. What does that give you? Then do the same for row two, [0,1].
Multiplying by [[2,0],[0,2]] just doubles the vector, right?
Test it on [3,5] — row one [2,0] dotted with [3,5], then row two [0,2] dotted with [3,5]. Do both entries come out doubled the way you'd expect?
What does it really mean for a matrix to 'act on' a vector?

Let's make it physical. Think of the matrix as a machine: you feed in a vector, and the machine reshapes the whole grid of space — stretching or rotating it — then hands you back where your vector landed. Two rules the machine never breaks: the center point stays fixed, and straight lines never bend. Given those rules, if you fed in the vector sitting right at the origin, where would it come back out?
Why do we only need to know where [1,0] and [0,1] go to know the whole transformation?

Think of [1,0] and [0,1] as two master keys. Every other vector is built from copies of those two — [3,2] is just three of the first plus two of the second. So once the machine tells you where both master keys land, you can rebuild where anything lands. Try it: if [1,0] goes to [2,0] and [0,1] goes to [0,5], where should [3,2] end up?
A transformation that flips everything across the x-axis isn't linear, since it changes signs.

Changing signs doesn't disqualify it — a reflection across the x-axis is perfectly linear. Run the two-rule check: does the origin stay put under that flip, and do straight lines stay straight? If both hold, what's your verdict?
Under the matrix with columns [1,1] and [-1,1], where does [1,0] go? Just need it.
It goes to [1,1] — the first column is exactly the landing spot of the [1,0] master key.
Why does the determinant use that criss-cross ad minus bc pattern?

Let's sneak up on it. The two columns of your matrix are the two edges of a parallelogram sitting at the origin, and the determinant measures that shape's area. Start with the easiest case, [[a,0],[0,d]]: the shape is just a rectangle with sides a and d. What's its area? Once you have that, we'll see where the minus-bc correction comes in as the shape tilts.

One sign slip: the determinant subtracts the second product, it doesn't add — so it's 1·4 − 2·2 = 4 − 4 = 0, not 8. And that zero isn't a dead end, it's telling you something: the two columns fall on the same line, flattening the parallelogram's area to nothing. Can you spot how [2,4] relates to [1,2]?
I have zero intuition for what an eigenvector actually is.

Set the formulas aside. Picture a long escalator. Most things placed on it get carried diagonally, off to a new spot. But a marble rolled exactly along the direction of the rails just travels farther along that same rail — never veering sideways. An eigenvector is like that rail direction under a transformation: it only gets lengthened or shortened along itself, never redirected. With that picture, what do you think the eigenvalue is measuring about the marble's trip?
For the identity matrix, I think only [1,0] and [0,1] are eigenvectors.

The identity is far more generous than that — actually every vector is an eigenvector here. Reason it out: since the identity leaves every vector exactly where it is, does ANY direction get knocked off its line, or does every single line survive untouched? And what eigenvalue matches 'left exactly as-is'?
Why isn't the rank of a matrix just how many numbers it has?

Let's ground rank in something physical. Picture each row of the matrix as a rope laid out on the floor, each pointing some direction. Rank counts how many ropes point in genuinely different directions — if two ropes lie exactly along the same line, they only count once between them. So if I handed you three ropes but two of them lay perfectly on top of each other, how many distinct directions would you really have?
For [[1,3],[2,6]] I counted 4 entries so I said rank 4.

Rank isn't about counting entries — it's about independent directions, and here it's actually 1, not 4. Check it: is row two, [2,6], just row one, [1,3], doubled? If one row is a scaled copy of the other, how many truly independent rows are you left with?
Does a matrix of all zeros have rank zero?
Reason it through the 'independent directions' idea — if every row is just the zero vector, pointing nowhere at all, how many genuine directions have you actually got to count?
I can't picture what the span of two vectors looks like.

Let's build it with your hands. Imagine two garden hoses fixed at one end to the same tap, each pointing a different way, and you can stretch each to any length. Every spot on the lawn you could reach by combining some stretch of one then the other — that whole reachable patch is the span. If both hoses point in clearly different directions on a flat lawn, how much of the lawn do you think you can eventually cover?
The span of [1,1] and [2,2] is the whole plane since they're two vectors.

Two vectors alone don't guarantee the whole plane — these two need a closer look. Is [2,2] just [1,1] stretched to double? If it is, do they open up two different directions, or stay stuck along the same single line?
If one of my two vectors is the zero vector, does that shrink the span?
Think of the zero vector as a hose with no length at all — no matter how you 'stretch' it, it reaches nowhere. So does it add any new territory beyond what your other single hose already covers?
How is a basis different from just any set that spans?

Let's test the difference on a simple case. Directions 'east' and 'north' let you describe any spot on a map — that's spanning. Now toss in 'northeast' as a third required direction: does it reach any new spot you couldn't already, or is it just a combo of east and north? What does your answer suggest a basis insists on that a plain spanning set doesn't?
I think [2,0] and [4,0] form a basis for the plane.

Both of those point along the exact same line — the x-axis — so they're more like two rulers laid end to end than two independent directions, which means they can't be a basis for the plane. Test the gap: can either of them ever reach a point off the x-axis, like (0,1)?
Does the standard basis have to be [1,0] and [0,1], or can other pairs work?

Picture setting up your own grid on graph paper — must your two reference directions be the horizontal and vertical, or could you tilt them, as long as they still branch in two different directions? What's the real requirement hiding under 'standard'?
Is [1,2] and [2,4] a basis for the plane? I said yes.
It's actually not — [2,4] is exactly [1,2] doubled, so both lie on one line and can't branch out to cover the plane. A basis needs two genuinely independent directions.
How can I tell if two vectors are perpendicular just from their numbers?

Let's link it to a tool you already trust. The dot product measures how much two vectors overlap in direction. If two vectors are perpendicular — sharing no common direction at all — how much overlap would you expect, and what single number would capture 'no overlap'? Try that number out as your test.
I think [1,2] and [2,1] are orthogonal since they look symmetric.
Looking symmetric isn't the test — and these two actually aren't orthogonal. Their dot product is 1·2 + 2·1 = 4, not zero. Can you see how a nonzero result rules out a right angle between them?
If two vectors point in the same direction, their dot product is definitely not zero, right?
Picture two people walking side by side the exact same way — maximum agreement in heading. Would their 'overlap' number sit at zero, or as far from zero as it gets?
I don't understand what projecting one vector onto another gives me.

Picture a flashlight held straight above a table. Hold a pencil at an angle over the surface — its shadow on the table is shorter than the pencil itself, and it lies flat along the table. That shadow is the projection: the part of the pencil that lies along the table's direction. So if you laid the pencil flat against the table already, how would its shadow compare to the pencil itself?
Projection of [0,4] onto [1,0] — I said [0,4] stays the same.
Not quite — projecting onto [1,0] keeps only the part lying along the x-axis, and [0,4] points straight up the y-axis with nothing along x. So how much of it survives the shadow onto the x-direction?
Is the projection always a scaled version of the vector I'm projecting onto?

Use the shadow picture — it always lands flat along the target direction, never off to the side. So if the projection must lie exactly along that one direction, what does that force it to be, relative to the vector you projected onto?
Just give me the projection of [3,7] onto [0,1].
It's [0,7] — projecting onto the y-axis keeps the y-part and drops the x-part, so only the 7 survives the shadow.
Do two vectors always span a plane?
Let's check with a quick test. Take [1,0] and [3,0] — both pointing along the x-axis. Can you combine them to reach the point (0,1), up off the axis?
No... any mix of them still stays on the x-axis.
Exactly. So what condition do two vectors need to meet before they can open up a whole plane instead of just a line?
Does adding more rows to a matrix always raise its rank?
Let's test it. Start with one row, [1,2] — that's rank 1. Now add a second row that happens to be [2,4]. Is that new row a fresh direction, or a scaled copy of the first?
It's just double the first row.
Right — so did the rank climb to 2, or hold at 1? And what does that tell you about whether more rows automatically means more rank?
How would I even spot an eigenvector by looking?

Picture the escalator rails again. For the matrix [[3,0],[0,1]], which stretches x by 3 and leaves y alone, think about the vector [1,0]. After the transformation, does it still point along its own line?
Yeah, it just gets three times longer but stays on the x-axis.
Exactly — so [1,0] is an eigenvector. Given it tripled in length without ever turning, what's its eigenvalue?
Is every pair of different vectors orthogonal?
Quick test: compute [1,1]·[1,0] — that's 1·1 + 1·0. Does it come out to zero?
It's 1, not zero.

Right — so these two aren't orthogonal even though they're clearly different vectors. What does that tell you about whether 'different' is enough, or whether orthogonality specifically needs the dot product to hit zero?
Does subtracting vectors work like adding them?
Let's test with a walk. If [5,3] is where you end up and [2,1] is a leg you already walked, [5,3]-[2,1] asks 'what's the remaining leg?' What do you get subtracting component by component?
Exactly. So subtraction is just 'what's left to walk' — can you say in a line why it's the same as adding the reverse of [2,1]?
What's a unit vector actually good for?

Think of a unit vector as a pure compass heading — it tells you which way without committing to how far. Once you have a clean heading, you can scale it to any distance you like. So if you wanted to point the same way as [3,4] but with length exactly 1, what would you need to divide [3,4] by?
Length of [5,12]? Just the number.
It's 13 — √(5² + 12²) = √169, one of those clean right-triangle triples.
The zero vector [0,0] points to the right by default, doesn't it?
It actually has no direction at all — picture an arrow with zero length; there's no way it can point anywhere. That's exactly what makes the zero vector a special case whenever direction matters.
Why is the dot product a single number and not another vector?

Think of it as a 'compatibility score' between two directions — one summary number, like rating how well two dance partners' steps line up. If it stayed a vector, it wouldn't be a score anymore. Given it's a score of alignment, what would the highest possible score situation look like for two arrows?
[1,1]·[1,1] is 1, right, since it's the same vector?
Same vector doesn't mean the answer is 1 — it's 1·1 + 1·1 = 2. Re-add the two products slowly and you'll see the 2.
Does the order matter — is a·b the same as b·a?
Picture two people shaking hands: does the 'agreement' between them change depending on who reached out first? Test it: is [2,3]·[4,1] the same as [4,1]·[2,3]?
Both give 8+3 = 11.
Right, identical. So what property of ordinary multiplication is quietly guaranteeing that the dot product doesn't care about order?
Just give me [3,4]·[4,3].
Why would anyone care about the dot product in machine learning?

Here's a comparison: imagine each data point is a list of traits, and you want to know how similar two points are. The dot product is like laying the two lists side by side and rewarding every place they agree. A high total means 'these two are alike'; near zero means 'unrelated.' Given that, why might a model use dot products to measure how well an input matches a stored pattern?
[2,5]·[3,1] — I did 2·3 and 5·1 and then multiplied them, so 6·5 = 30.
Close on the two products, but the last step combines them by adding, not multiplying — so it's 6 + 5 = 11, not 30. Try that final add instead and see.
What does multiplying two matrices together actually represent?

Picture two machines on an assembly line: the vector goes through machine B first, then machine A. The product AB is a single combined machine that does both stages in one pass. So if B rotates and A stretches, what does the combined machine AB do to something fed into it?
For [[1,1],[0,1]] times [2,0], is the result [2,0]?
Check row one, [1,1], dotted with [2,0] — what's 1·2 + 1·0?
That's 2. And row two, [0,1] dotted with [2,0], is 0.
Exactly — [2,0]. Since the input had a zero second component, the shear didn't visibly move it. What kind of input WOULD reveal the shear?
Please just tell me [[1,2],[3,4]] times [2,1].
It's [4,10] — row one gives 1·2+2·1=4, row two gives 3·2+4·1=10.
Why can't I multiply a 2x3 matrix by another 2x3 matrix?

Think of matrices as adapters with plugs and sockets. The right matrix outputs a certain number of prongs; the left matrix has a socket expecting a certain number. They only connect when the prongs match the socket — the inner dimensions have to agree. So for A times B, which dimension of A has to match which dimension of B for the plug to fit?
[[1,0],[2,1]] times [3,4] — I got [3,4], unchanged.
Row one is fine (gives 3), but row two isn't the identity here — [2,1] dotted with [3,4] is 2·3 + 1·4 = 10, not 4. So the result is [3,10]. That extra 2 in the corner is doing real work.
How do I know the size of the matrix I get after multiplying?

Picture the outer edges of the two matrices as the frame of the result. Multiply a 2x3 by a 3x2 and the leftover outer numbers — the 2 and the 2 — frame the answer. Using that rule, what size do you get multiplying a 3x2 by a 2x4?
What does a 90-degree rotation matrix do to the basic arrows?

Picture spinning the whole grid a quarter turn counterclockwise. The arrow [1,0] pointing east swings up to point north. Where do you think the north-pointing arrow [0,1] lands after that same quarter turn?
How do I find where a specific vector lands under a transformation?
Let's use the columns as landing spots. Say [1,0] lands at [2,0] and [0,1] lands at [1,3]. For the vector [1,1], how many of each landing spot do you combine?
One of each, so [2,0] + [1,3]?
Exactly — now add those to get the final landing point.
Scaling everything by 3 can't be linear — it's too simple to count.

Simplicity doesn't disqualify it — uniform scaling by 3 is a textbook linear transformation. It keeps the origin fixed and keeps straight lines straight, which are the only two requirements. Can you picture why tripling every coordinate leaves (0,0) exactly where it is?
Matrix with columns [2,1] and [0,3] — where does [1,0] land? Just the answer.
It lands at [2,1] — the first column is precisely where the [1,0] flag gets sent.
det([[3,1],[2,4]]) — how do I set it up?
Use the criss-cross: main diagonal product minus the other diagonal product. That's 3·4 minus 1·2. What single number does that come out to?
Does scaling a matrix scale its determinant the same way?
Let's test with area. det([[1,0],[0,1]]) is 1. Now double every entry to get [[2,0],[0,2]] — compute that determinant.
Right, 4, not 2. Doubling both edges of the unit square multiplied the area by 4. What does that suggest about why the determinant didn't just double?
Just tell me det([[2,3],[1,4]]).
Determinants are always positive since they measure area, right?

Area itself is positive, but the determinant can go negative — the sign also records whether the transformation flipped the space over, like a mirror. Try det([[0,1],[1,0]]): what sign do you get, and can you picture the flip it's describing?
What would a determinant mean for a 3x3 matrix?

Step up one dimension in your imagination. In 2D the determinant was the area of the parallelogram from the columns. In 3D, picture the three columns as the edges of a slanted box — a parallelepiped. What quantity of that box do you think the 3x3 determinant is now measuring, by analogy to area?
If an eigenvalue is 2, what's physically happening to that eigenvector?
Picture the marble on its rail again — the eigenvalue is the stretch factor along that rail. With an eigenvalue of 2, how much longer does the eigenvector get, and does it stay on its own line?
Eigenvalues of [[5,0],[0,-3]] — just confirm them.
They're 5 and -3 — for a diagonal matrix the diagonal entries are the eigenvalues, each the stretch (or flip, for the negative) along its own axis.
How do I check whether [1,1] is an eigenvector of [[2,0],[0,2]]?
Multiply the matrix by [1,1] and see where it lands. Row one gives 2·1+0·1, row two gives 0·1+2·1 — what vector comes out?
Right. Is [2,2] just a scaled copy of [1,1]? If so, [1,1] is an eigenvector — what's the eigenvalue?
For [[0,1],[1,0]], I think [1,0] is an eigenvector since it's a simple axis vector.

Being a simple axis vector isn't enough — multiply [[0,1],[1,0]] by [1,0] and you get [0,1], which points a totally new way, so it got redirected, not just scaled. Try [1,1] instead: where does that land, and does it stay on its own line?
Why do people say a low-rank matrix 'loses information'?

Think of rank as how many independent dials the transformation really has. If a 3-input transformation only has 2 independent dials, one input's worth of information gets folded into the others and can't be recovered. Given that, what would a rank-1 transformation be doing to all its inputs?
Rank of [[2,4],[3,6]] — I said 2.
It's actually 1 — row two, [3,6], is exactly 1.5 times row one, [2,4], so there's only one independent direction despite it being a full 2x2.
Can a matrix with more rows than columns still have high rank?

Rank can't exceed the smaller dimension — picture ropes in a 2D room: no matter how many ropes you lay down, they can only point in at most 2 independent directions there. So for a 5x2 matrix, what's the ceiling on its rank?
2, since there are only 2 columns.
Exactly. So what limits rank — the count of rows, or the smaller of rows and columns?
Is the identity matrix always full rank?
Check its rows: for [[1,0],[0,1]], do [1,0] and [0,1] point in genuinely different directions, or is one a copy of the other? What does that make the rank?
Can three vectors in 2D span more than two vectors could?

Picture the flat lawn again — two hoses in different directions already reach every spot on it. Adding a third hose on that same flat lawn: does it unlock any new ground, or is it just another route to places you could already reach? What does that say about the extra vector?
Does [2,0] and [0,3] span the whole plane? Yes or no.
Yes — they point in two different directions (along each axis), and any point (a,b) can be mixed from the right amounts of each.
If two vectors are parallel, what's their span?
Test it: take [1,2] and [2,4]. Is the second a scaled copy of the first?
Yes, it's double.
Right. So when both point along the same line, what shape does every combination of them trace — a plane, or just that one line?
I don't understand why span is called 'all linear combinations.'

Think of it like a smoothie bar with two base ingredients. A 'linear combination' is any smoothie you make: some amount of ingredient one plus some amount of ingredient two. The span is the entire menu of every smoothie you could ever blend from those two. So if your two ingredients were arrows, what would the 'menu' correspond to geometrically?
How do I check if two vectors form a basis for the plane?
